nameStory: Rostania occultata gets its species name from the Latin word 'occultata,' meaning 'hidden' or 'concealed.' This tiny lichen truly lives up to its name, being so rare and inconspicuous that it's easily overlooked even by experienced lichen hunters. The genus Rostania honors botanist Rostan, though this secretive species seems to prefer staying out of the spotlight!
description: Rostania occultata is an extremely rare, small gelatinous lichen that forms tiny, dark patches on its preferred surfaces. When dry, it appears as thin, blackish crusts that might be mistaken for dirt or staining, but when moistened it transforms into a more obvious, somewhat translucent greenish-black film. This lichen belongs to the jelly lichen family, meaning it swells and becomes gelatinous when wet. Individual colonies rarely exceed a few centimeters across, making it one of our most diminutive and elusive lichens.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, film-like patches that feel almost papery when dry but become soft and gelatinous when wet, like touching a thin piece of wet seaweed

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark blackish-brown when dry, transforming to translucent greenish-black or olive when moistened, with the color change happening within minutes of wetting

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny colonies typically 1-3 centimeters across, often forming irregular patches that could easily be overlooked as mere discoloration

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth and somewhat shiny when wet, but dry specimens feel brittle and may crack or flake when gently touched

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring the protected undersides of branches or trunk crevices where moisture lingers

habitat: This extremely rare lichen inhabits the bark of deciduous trees in humid, sheltered locations throughout New England's forests. It seems to prefer smooth-barked trees like maples or birches, typically growing in protected spots where morning dew and light rain can keep it moist longer. Look for it in mature forests with good canopy cover, particularly in valleys or north-facing slopes where humidity stays higher.

seasonality.spring: Most visible during wet spring weather when frequent rain keeps the lichen hydrated and displaying its characteristic greenish-black color. This is often the best time to spot it as it's most obvious when gelatinous.
seasonality.summer: May appear completely dried out and blackish during hot, dry periods, easily mistaken for bark staining. Early morning dew can temporarily rehydrate it, making dawn the best time to search.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains bring the lichen back to life after summer dormancy, and the increased moisture makes this another good season for detection. Falling leaves may temporarily cover colonies.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may be hidden under snow. During winter thaws and ice melts, the lichen can become quite prominent as it absorbs the available moisture.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region, making any new discovery potentially significant for science! It can survive being completely dried out for months, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet, like a botanical resurrection.
confusionNotes: When dry, it's easily mistaken for simple bark discoloration, fungal staining, or even dirt accumulation. The key test is to add a few drops of water - if it's Rostania occultata, it will quickly transform from a dark crust into a translucent, gelatinous film. Remember: 'When in doubt, add a drop' - real bark stains won't change texture when wetted.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that any potential sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanical organizations or iNaturalist, as new records could be scientifically valuable. Because it's so inconspicuous when dry, it may be more common than records suggest but simply overlooked by collectors.
compareHints: Since Rostania occultata is the only member of its genus known from New England, compare it to other small, dark gelatinous lichens in the jelly lichen family (Collemataceae). Unlike the more common Collema species which tend to form leafier, more obvious structures, Rostania occultata remains firmly film-like even when wet. Other dark, crusty lichens won't have the dramatic wet-to-dry transformation that makes this species unique.
